extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational creativity / NLP evaluating short story generation (LLMs vs humans)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of five-sentence short stories (cue-word task) using human judges (experts, non-experts), LLM judges, and automated metrics to assess creativity and related dimensions. Focuses on which metrics predict perceived creativity and differences between judge populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: creativity (rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity ratings (primary focus) collected on a 5-point scale; creativity ratings are highly correlated with originality, surprise, and effectiveness and used as the dependent variable for further analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper focuses solely on creativity ratings for analyses because creativity, originality, surprise and effectiveness are highly correlated. Experts rate human stories 1.25 points higher (scale of 5) than LLM stories; non-experts and LLM judges rate AI stories higher. Expert judgments correlate strongly with automated metrics (semantic diversity, surprise, lexical diversity). Use multiple raters (authors used two quasi-/expert raters and five non-experts) and report inter-rater reliability (reported correlations: experts .83–.89, non-experts .64–.74, LLMs .92–.99).

rubrics_metrics.name: originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is treated as a dimension highly correlated with creativity (mentioned alongside surprise and effectiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality scores correlate with creativity ratings and therefore are not modelled separately in main analyses; implicitly valued by expert judges as part of creative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise is used as an automated metric and human-judged dimension related to creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise is a positive predictor of expert creativity ratings (higher surprise → higher expert-rated creativity) but is negatively associated with creativity ratings from non-experts and LLM judges. Surprise metric is one of the predictors in regression models of creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness is listed as one of the dimensions (along with creativity, originality, surprise) that are highly correlated and used in initial rating collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because effectiveness correlates strongly with creativity and other dimensions, the authors focus further analyses on creativity alone; effectiveness functions as part of the consensual assessment battery.

rubrics_metrics.name: novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is operationalized by a reference-based metric (frequency-based uniqueness) used to assess how novel a story is relative to a reference corpus of stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty was used as a predictor in regression models; non-expert and LLM creativity ratings decrease with higher novelty in this dataset. Limitations: the novelty metric is reference-based and depends heavily on the chosen reference corpus (authors note this as a shortcoming of reference-based novelty assessments).

rubrics_metrics.name: semantic_diversity (inverse homogenization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic diversity measured using inverse homogenization (see Methods); used as the representative metric for lexical/semantic diversity in regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semantic diversity is the strongest positive predictor of expert creativity ratings. For non-experts and LLM judges, semantic diversity is negatively associated with rated creativity. Authors emphasize semantic diversity as essential to creativity per expert judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: lexical_diversity (mean n-gram diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexical diversity is measured using mean n-gram diversity of a story and used as the lexical diversity predictor in regression models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lexical diversity positively predicts expert creativity ratings (though effect sizes smaller than semantic diversity). Lexical diversity is one of the automated metrics correlated with human judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: lexical_complexity (number_of_unique_words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexical complexity operationalized as the number of unique words in a story; used to represent lexical complexity because many lexical/syntactic metrics were highly correlated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of unique words is the best positive predictor of creativity ratings for non-experts and LLM judges (i.e., non-experts and LLMs favor sheer lexical complexity). Authors note that high lexical complexity does not necessarily imply semantic complexity and LLMs tend to overuse rare adjectives and verbosity, creating an illusion of creativity for untrained judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: syntactic_complexity (average constituency tree depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntactic complexity represented by average constituency tree depth of sentences in a story; chosen as the single syntactic metric for regressions because syntactic metrics were highly correlated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LLMs show higher syntactic complexity than humans overall, but syntactic complexity was not a consistent positive predictor of creativity ratings across judge groups (small/negative or non-significant effects in regressions).

rubrics_metrics.name: readability / ease_of_reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Human stories are characterized as linguistically much less complex and easier to read; readability is discussed as a qualitative dimension that correlates with human preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not always formalized as a single metric in the paper, readability/ease-of-reading is highlighted as a desirable quality of human-written stories and contrasts with LLM verbosity and syntactic overload. Flesch (1940) is cited in references as a relevant readability reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: diversity (thematic and lexical/semantic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity includes lexical diversity, semantic diversity, and thematic diversity (number of themes); human stories exhibit higher lexical and semantic diversity and broader theme counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report that human stories consistently exhibit higher novelty, surprise, and lexical and semantic diversity, while LLM stories tend to focus on a few repetitive themes. Figure/Table analyses report the number of themes for human vs AI stories and dominant themes per item set.

rubrics_metrics.name: thematic_richness / number_of_themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Count / variety of themes present in a story (Figure 8 reports number of themes for human and AI stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human stories show more diverse and nuanced themes; AI stories often focus on a few repetitive or formulaic themes. Thematic richness is used as an analytic axis (qualitative coding summarized in Table 5 / Figure 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausibility is listed among qualities attributed by non-experts (human stories described as 'everyday life', 'mundane' vs AI described as 'fantastic', 'unrealistic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-experts associate plausibility with human-authored texts and associate implausibility/fantastical content with AI stories; plausibility informs author-detection strategies and perceived enjoyability.

rubrics_metrics.name: emotional_depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional depth (e.g., 'emotional', 'relatable', 'personal', 'first-person', 'evoking feelings', 'empathy') is a theme non-experts attribute to human stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional depth is cited as a desirable property that human stories tend to exhibit more than AI stories; non-experts often use perceived emotional depth as a cue for human authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbosity describes a style quality (AI stories described as 'verbose', 'wordy', 'elaborate', 'descriptive', with repeating phrases; human stories described as 'simple', 'shorter', 'to the point').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbosity is identified as a common LLM trait (possibly resulting from alignment/optimization) and can create an illusion of creativity for non-expert judges (verbosity bias). Authors cite verbosity bias literature and note LLMs' verbosity may reduce perceived novelty/diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: enjoyability
rubrics_metrics.description: Enjoyability / ease of following (e.g., 'more depth', 'more sense', 'rythmic', 'easier to follow', 'more enjoyable') is reported as a non-expert quality favoring human stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-experts rate enjoyable, easier-to-follow stories higher and often associate enjoyability with human authorship; used qualitatively in theme analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: human_vs_AI_detection (Turing Test accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge ability to correctly predict author (human or AI) of a story; reported accuracies: experts 94%, non-experts 81%, LLM judges 71%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a separate evaluation axis to measure whether LLMs can 'fool' judges. Authors gather non-expert explanations for how they predicted authorship and summarize themes used as cues (plausibility, verbosity, emotional depth, etc.). High expert accuracy suggests experts can reliably distinguish human vs AI in this setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: judge_population and rater_reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Different judge types (experts, non-experts, and LLM judges) show varying reliability and biases: experts are most reliable, non-experts less so, LLM judges biased toward AI generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter-rater correlations reported (experts .83–.89, non-experts .64–.74, LLMs .92–.99 for internal consistency across multiple dimensions). The authors recommend the minimum recommended number of raters used in their study (two quasi-/expert raters, five non-experts) but note more raters would improve reliability. Literature cited suggests quasi-experts may be as reliable as experts for some tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_automated_metrics_as_predictors (regression model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple explainable regression model predicts creativity ratings using one predictor from each automated-metric category (semantic_diversity, lexical_diversity, novelty, surprise, syntactic_complexity, lexical_complexity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors choose a single representative metric per category because many metrics are highly correlated. The regressions reveal different predictors for different judge groups (experts: semantic diversity, surprise, lexical diversity positive; non-experts/LLMs: lexical complexity positive, semantic diversity/novelty/surprise negative). This is guidance for metric selection and interpretation when modeling perceived creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: reference_based_novelty_limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that the novelty metric used is reference-based and depends heavily on the chosen reference corpus (the set of human- and AI-written stories for each item set in this study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors highlight this as a limitation of their novelty assessment and note that reference-based uniqueness is a common shortcoming in creativity research; recommend validating with larger/more diverse reference sets or alternative novelty measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: consensual_assessment_technique / expert_evaluation_standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of human expert judgments (consensual assessment tradition) to evaluate creativity, citing Amabile 1982 and related work about expert reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consensual assessment technique underpins the use of expert ratings as a gold-standard for creativity evaluation; authors rely on experts/quasi-experts as primary reliable judges and discuss literature supporting expert superiority and reliability.
